title: Effect of Microstructure and Surface Diffusion on Crack Resistance of Low-Carbon Steel Using Oil-Based CNT Nanofluid Quenching
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the limitations of quenching media in resisting crack propagation in low-carbon steel, particularly in relation to microstructural features and surface diffusion effects. A novel quenching medium was developed by incorporating carbon nanotube (CNT) into oil-based due to their excellent cooling properties. Specimens of low-carbon steel were prepared and heated at austenitization temperature for 1 hour followed by immersing into oil and oil-based CNT nanofluid. Both treated samples were polished delicately for microstructure and surface diffusion analysis with the untreated specimen served as a benchmark specimen. Further, the crack growth tests were carried out using compact tension (CT) specimen under constant amplitude loading (CAL). The results indicate that specimen quenched in oil-based CNT nanofluid provided the highest crack resistance and fatigue life at threshold value of (ΔK th ) 17.1 MPa√m and 34,464 cycles which is higher than those of the untreated and oil-based quenched specimens. This improvement is attributed to different formation of coarse and fine upper bainite, grain size boundaries dislocation, and the presence layer depth of surface diffusion at 34 µm. Overall, the CNT-infused oil enhances heat transfer efficiency during quenching, effectively retarding crack propagation and extending fatigue life.
journal: Journal of Failure Analysis and Prevention

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Since the beginning of the twenty-first century, steel has remained one of the most widely used metals in across various industries due to its affordability, versatility, and excellent workability. Steel is an iron-carbon alloy, containing varying amounts of carbon that is typically classified into low-, medium-, and high-carbon steels [ 1 ,  2 ]. Within this category, low-carbon steel, containing less than 0.25wt.% carbon, is the most extensively produced type of steel each year [ 3 ] and is widely employed in developed countries such as Germany and China [ 4 ,  5 ]. However, the extensive use of low-carbon steel has raised concerns among researchers regarding its structural performance, particularly after conventional quenching, which can lead to residual stresses and surface defects that promote fatigue failure and crack growth.

Cyclic loading is referred to the repeated and fluctuating stresses and strains experienced by a material, which can lead to the initiation and propagation of fatigue cracks over time [ 6 ]. As a result, the strength and service life of the material decrease. However, this crack growth can be delayed when certain conditions change, such as grain size refinement [ 7 ], microstructural control [ 8 ], the presence of crack-tip shielding mechanisms, or when the stress intensity factor drops below a critical value which is also known as fatigue threshold, ΔK th  [ 9 ]. This phenomenon is referred to as crack resistance. Achieving fatigue crack resistance is crucial in structure integrity to prevent sudden catastrophic structural failures.

In industrial applications, quenching is a common method employed to enhance the mechanical properties of low-carbon steel. Conventional quenching media such as water, oil, and brine used for quenching treatment, and fundamentally influences the bulk microstructure and surface diffusion layer of steel. The microstructure refers to spatial arrangement of phases, grain size, grain boundaries, and imperfections within the steel at the nanometer to micrometer scale [ 10 ], whereas surface diffusion describes the movement of atoms along the surface or within the shallow subsurface region [ 11 ]. Both phenomena can be systematically examined using the microscopy and composition analysis. Recently, many researchers [ 12 ,  13 – 14 ] have focused on using nanofluids as quenching media, particularly the combination of carbon nanotube (CNT) and oil-based fluids. In such systems, the microstructure and surface diffusion play a critical role in determining the mechanical behavior of steel. To name a few, factors such as phase composition, grain size, and common elements that undergo surface diffusion including carbon, hydrogen, and alloying elements significantly influence the mechanical properties of quenched steels. For instance, [ 15 ,  16 ] reported that quenching promotes the formation of tougher and harder phases, thereby enhancing the local strength and hardness of low-carbon steel, which can theoretically deflect and impede crack growth. Lan et al. [ 17 ], further noted that grain refinement during quenching increases grain boundary density, which acts as an effective barrier to crack propagation. Moreover, a study by Sun et al. demonstrated that the steel surface at elevated temperatures promotes atomic migration along and into the steel surface, enhancing interfacial bonding between the surface layer and the substrate through gradual compositional and microstructural transition. Although improvements in mechanical properties through CNT-based nanofluid quenching media have been reported, the combined effects on crack resistance have not been fully explored. This knowledge gap limits the development of advanced quenching techniques aimed at producing optimized phase composition, refined grain size, and increased depth of surface diffusion layer, thereby improving the crack resistance in low-carbon steel.

This study specifically demonstrates that the microstructure transformation and surface diffusion induced by oil-based CNT nanofluid quenching have the potential to be recognized as an advanced and effective quenching medium for enhancing the properties of low-carbon steel. The main objective is to improve crack resistance and extend the total fatigue life of low-carbon steel. The untreated specimen was used as the baseline, while the conventional oil-quenched specimen served as a comparative oil-based control. The microstructure and surface diffusion were examined using microscopy and energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS) techniques. Crack growth behavior was experimentally assessed using compact tension (CT) specimens under constant amplitude loading (CAL), and the results for the untreated, oil, and oil-based CNT nanofluid-quenched steels were analyzed and discussed within the Paris region, correlating crack growth rate with the stress intensity factor range (∆K).

sections.heading: Specimens Preparation
paragraphs: This study used a material low-carbon steel containing 0.17% of carbon with its chemical composition presented in Table  1 . The material was selected due to its relatively low austenite transformation temperature (Ac 1  ≈ 727 °C) and full austenitization temperature which is near to 870 °C [ 18 ]. The quenching procedure involved heating the specimens to 900 °C, approximately 20–30 °C above the Ac 3  temperature, and holding for 60 minutes to ensure complete transformation from ferrite to full austenite. Subsequently, the specimens were immediately immersed in conventional oil and oil-based CNT nanofluid until thermal equilibrium was achieved which allowing the specimens to pass through the critical cooling rate for complete heat extraction and stabilization of internal thermal stresses [ 19 ]. These oil-based quenching media were adopted due to their lower cooling rates compared to water-quenching medium, which helps minimize thermal shock, residual stresses, while promoting the formation of hard and tough microstructures [ 20 ]. The addition of CNT in the nanofluid is intended to enhance surface heat transfer and facilitate phase transformation, promote grain refinement, and influence the depth of the surface diffusion layer during quenching. All specimens were mechanically polished to remove any damaged layer or oxide layers prior to analysis. sections.heading: Preparation and Stability of CNT Nanofluid
paragraphs: In this study, two quenching media were used: conventional oil and an oil-based carbon nanotube (CNT) nanofluid, whose characteristics are summarized in Table  2 . The preparation of the CNT nanofluid followed the method mentioned by Mubasyir et al. [ 21 ] by dispersing carbon nanotubes at a concentration of 0.1 wt.% CNT into 400 ml of base oil. The dispersion process was conducted in two stages to ensure homogeneity. Initially, the oil-based CNT nanofluid underwent ultrasonic bath agitation for 15 minutes to disrupt large agglomerates [ 22 ]. This was followed by probe ultrasonication at 40% amplitude for 40 minutes using a pulse mode of 5 seconds ON and 3 seconds OFF, while maintaining the fluid temperature below 40 °C [ 23 ]. Following this, the stability and dispersion of the CNT nanofluid were assessed before and after ultrasonication, as shown in Fig.  1 . Prior to ultrasonication, significant CNT agglomeration was observed within the base conventional oil. After ultrasonication, the dispersion showed a clear reduction in agglomerate size and a more uniform CNT distribution. This indicates improved dispersion stability and maintains more consistent cooling conditions during quenching process. The quality of CNT dispersion has a direct impact on thermal conductivity [ 14 ]. The well-dispersed CNT significantly enhances cooling uniformity during quenching by facilitating rapid heat pathways, which in turn promotes finer structures and inhibits excessive ferrite grain growth in steel. This scientific justification highlights the necessity for accurate dispersion and stability methods. sections.heading: Microstructure Image and Hardness Preparation
paragraphs: Metallographic specimens were prepared in accordance with ASTM E3 following the procedure reported by Muñoz-Rodenas et al. [ 24 ] for microstructural analysis after the quenching process. The cross sections of different low-carbon steel samples, including untreated, conventional oil, and oil-based CNT nanofluid-quenched conditions were sectioned and securely mounted using hot compressing molding. Manual grinding was carried out under water lubrication using silicon carbide (SiC) abrasive papers with various grit sizes ranging from 180, 320, 600, 800, 1200, and 2000 [ 25 ]. Between each successive grit, the specimens were rotate 90° to ensure the progressive removal of surface deformation from preceding stage. Mechanical polishing was then performed on a rotating disk at a speed of 300 RPM using 0.5 µm alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) suspension on a synthetic velvet cloth. This step was maintained for approximately 5–10 minutes per sample until a mirror-like surface was achieved [ 25 ]. Between each grinding and mechanical polishing stage, the specimens were thoroughly rinsed with distilled water and ethanol to avoid cross-contamination of abrasives and any residual polishing media from the surface prior to etching. The polished samples were then etched with 5% Nital (nitric acid ethanol), and each polished probe was submerged for 6 seconds. Upon completion, the samples were washed with distilled water and examined by optical microscopy. These observations were used to characterize metallurgical changes such as phase transformation, grain refinement, and surface hardening effects.

Additionally, surface diffusion behavior was analyzed in the near-surface region of the cross section, where the microstructure revealed the variation in depth of hardened surface layer and carbon enrichment due to different cooling rates and possible carbon adsorption from CNT nanofluid as quenching medium [ 26 ]. These features were expand investigated using EDS line scans and microscopy image to quantify diffusion depth caused by different of cooling media during quenching. A schematic illustration is provided in Fig.  2  to visually summarize the phase transformation process, refined grain morphology, and layer depth of surface diffusion induced by CNT nanofluid at the cross section of specimen. Fig. 2 Schematic illustration of phase transformation process, refined grain morphology, and depth of surface diffusion at the cross section with the molded sample dimensions (in mm)

In parallel, hardness profiling across the diffusion depth was evaluated on same polished cross section using Vickers microhardness testing (HV0.025) with a 25-gf load and dwell time of 15 seconds, in accordance with ASTM E384 and following a previous study [ 27 ]. Microhardness testing was selected due to its suitability for characterizing the surface hardness of materials that are typically small in size, thin surface layers, and require measurement accuracy that cannot be performed using macrohardness method. An example microhardness measurement on untreated condition was taken from surface toward the core to calculate the hardness profile across diffusion depth as shown in Fig.  3 . The first indentation was taken at 20 µm from the surface and was considered as the hardness of the surface, and measurements were continued up to 100 µm as the initial hardness of the core. The case profiles obtained were based on the average hardness values with three repetitions for both untreated and treated samples. Therefore, these combined observations microstructure phase, depth of surface diffusion, and hardness profile form the basis for interpreting the improvements in crack resistance of low-carbon steel. Fig. 3 Microhardness measurement on the cross section of the untreated sample showing the indentation points and measurement distance from the surface across the diffusion depth

sections.heading: Crack Growth Test Preparation
paragraphs: Compact tension (CT) specimens were fabricated following the guidelines set forth in ASTM E647. The specimens exhibited a width (W) of 50 mm, a thickness (B) of 6 mm, and an initial notch length (a) of 12.5 mm, as illustrated in Fig.  4 . Crack growth tests were performed using a 100 kN servo-hydraulic testing machine. The tests were conducted under constant amplitude loading (CAL) at a frequency of 10 Hz and a load ratio of R = 0.1, maintained at room temperature [ 28 ]. The crack length ( a ) was measured at intervals of 0.0025 mm in relation to the number of cycles ( N f ) for both untreated and quenched specimens subjected to Mode I loading conditions [ 29 ]. A crack opening displacement (COD) clip gauge was installed at the notch mouth to measure real-time displacement at the crack tip during the cyclic loading process, utilizing the compliance technique [ 29 ]. The displacement measurements were correlated with the applied stress intensity factor range (ΔK), which served as the input for Paris law analysis and associated fracture mechanics evaluations. The process flow of this study is summarized in Fig.  5 . Fig. 4 Crack growth setup ( a ) COD placement on specimen and ( b ) CT specimen geometry (in mm) Fig. 5 The flow of the study

sections.heading: Crack Growth Analysis
Microstructure Image Analysis
paragraphs: Typical optical microstructures illustrating phase transformation and grain structure before and after quenching treatments are presented in Table  3  and Fig.  6 . Figure  7  summarizes the effect of untreated, conventional oil, and oil-based CNT nanofluid quenching on average grain size with standard deviation, measured using the linear intercept measurements [ 30 ]. For each specimen, a total intercept length of 8834 µm was analyzed to ensure measurement reliability. The findings clearly show that the microstructure refinement was strongly influenced by the type of quenching medium, primarily due to different cooling rate behavior. The untreated steel exhibited a relatively soft and ductile structure, comprising approximately 30% pearlite and 70% ferrite, with an average grain size of 21 ± 0.99 µm, whereas conventional oil quenching reduced the average grain size to 12 ± 0.42 µm and produced a core microstructure dominated by coarser ferrite, with the presence of 40% coarser upper bainite in small amounts. The cooling rate at the core was insufficient to facilitate martensite formation, allowing more time for the development and growth of other phases compared to the rapid transformations achieved through faster quenching techniques [ 31 ]. The addition of CNT particles into the base oil considerably further refined the smallest grain size to 10 ± 0.27 µm and promoted the formation of fine upper bainite with fine ferrite remaining the dominant phase in the microstructure. The higher thermal conductivity of the CNT-based nanofluid increased the cooling rate and restricted ferrite grain growth during transformation [ 15 ]. In addition, CNT at the quench interface improved heat extraction uniformity [ 32 ], indirectly enhancing bainitic transformation and grain size refinement. These microstructural changes characterized by refined size of grain and increased grain boundary density together with bainitic morphology phase, which act as an effective barriers to crack propagation. sections.heading: Surface Diffusion Analysis
paragraphs: The dynamics of surface diffusion in quenched steel are influenced by the cooling rate, the mobility of carbon, and the behavior of transformations occurring specifically at near the surface. In the process of rapid heat extraction, carbon atoms from the quenching are adsorbed onto the specimen surface and subsequently migrate into the austenite through interstitial diffusion, resulting in a carbon-enriched diffusion zone. The depth and concentration of this zone are influenced by the thermal gradient as well as the chemical environment of the quenching medium.

Figure  8  shows the cross-sectional image EDS mapping and the depth of surface diffusion at 500x magnification. The listed wt.% values represent the average carbon and iron concentrations (by mass fraction) obtained from EDS area analysis, while the accompanying ± σ values denote the statistical variability (standard deviation) of the measurements. The untreated specimen, serving as the baseline, showed 1.7 ± 0.5 wt.% carbon with no observable diffusion depth layer, confirming the absence of external carbon migration in the as-received state. In the oil-quenched specimen, the surface carbon content slightly increased to 1.9 ± 0.4 wt.%, with a near-surface zone extending to approximately 20 µm in depth. This zone formed due to cooling rate-driven phase transformation gradients during quenching, consistent with previous observations [ 33 ] that quenching media influence surface diffusion in the near-surface microstructural region. The carbon enrichment at the surface induced by adsorption of carbon-containing species from hydrocarbon composition of the oil limited short-range diffusion into the austenite during the brief elevated temperature stage prior to transformation. Fig. 8 Cross-sectional image of EDS mapping analysis and layer depth of surface diffusion ( a ) before quenching, ( b ) after conventional oil quenching, and ( c ) after oil-based CNT nanofluid quenching

More significantly, the specimen quenched in oil-based CNT nanofluid exhibited the highest surface carbon concentration reaching 2.5 ± 0.5 wt.% and deepest surface diffusion layer of approximately 34 µm, exceeding conventional oil quenching. This improvement is attributed to the enhance thermal conductivity of the CNT nanofluid, which increases the cooling rate and promotes more uniform heat extraction [ 15 ]. As a result, the surface experiences a steeper transformation gradient, producing highest depth of the hardened surface layer [ 34 ]. From diffusion perspective, a modified depth roughly in the range of a few 10 µm is physically plausible for interstitial carbon in austenite during short-high-temperature exposure, consistent with diffusion length scaling x ∼ √Dt using literature diffusivities for carbon in austenite [ 11 ]. The presence of CNT particles in the oil also facilitates carbon adsorption from decomposed hydrocarbons and potentially release carbon at high temperatures [ 35 ], leading to slight surface carbon enrichment. Additionally, the EDS spectra confirmed that the elemental distribution obtained from the mapping analysis. The relatively narrow ± σ values reflect consistent spectral intensity across the scanned region, indicating uniformity of the local carbon enrichment at the measured depths. Therefore, this performance aligns with empirical observation that CNT acts not only as a heat transfer medium but also as a carbon contributor especially at temperatures where surface energy interactions between CNT and the steel matrix become favorable.

sections.heading: Hardness Across Surface Diffusion Depth
paragraphs: The hardness profile across surface diffusion depth after quenching in different cooling media was analyzed by the Vickers hardness measurement method. The microhardness variation with depth is presented in Table  4  and Fig.  9 , providing a quantitative validation of the surface enhancement for each quenching medium. The untreated specimen exhibits a stable and uniform hardness across the measured depth, ranging from 151 HV ± 16.9 to 152 HV ± 14.3. This consistency confirms the baseline property of the steel in its as-received state, characterized by a typical ferrite–pearlite matrix [ 36 ]. In contrast, both quenched specimens display a clear hardness gradient, where the highest values are recorded near the surface and gradually decrease toward the core material. This gradient is characteristic of diffusion-affected hardened layer, where rapid heat extraction during quenching modifies the near-surface microstructure. Table 4 Vickers hardness values across surface diffusion depth at cross section for untreated and quenched specimens Measurement point Depth from surface (µm) Untreated (HV) Conventional oil (HV) Oil-based CNT nanofluid (HV) 1 20 153 ± 17.9 183 ± 16.8 218 ± 14.2 2 30 155 ± 12.2 176 ± 24.1 213 ± 20.3 3 40 151 ± 16.9 170 ± 21.5 202 ± 16.6 4 60 154 ± 10.8 166 ± 23.9 176 ± 19.8 5 80 150 ± 10.0 162 ± 24.8 163 ± 21.4 6 100 152 ± 14.3 160 ± 19.4 161 ± 15.1 Fig. 9 Hardness profile across diffusion depth for specimen untreated, conventional oil, and oil-based CNT nanofluid quenched

For the conventional oil-quenched specimen, the hardness reaches 183 HV ± 16.8 at a depth 20 µm, which represents a significant increase over untreated condition. However, as the distance from the surface increases, the hardness values progressively decrease, reaching 160 ± 19.4 at 100 µm. This value can be considered as the core hardness of the quenched specimen [ 27 ]. The increase in core hardness relative to the untreated steel is attributed to bulk microstructural refinement and the formation of hard bainite phases during the heat and quenching process [ 31 ].

A more pronounced hardening effect is observed in the oil-based CNT nanofluid-quenched specimen, which demonstrates a highest surface hardness, achieving a peak hardness of 218 HV ± 14.2 at 20 µm. This represents a significant improvement compared with the conventional oil-quenched specimen at the same depth, which highlighting the dual role of carbon nanotubes as both a superior heat transfer medium and a supplemental carbon source during quenching. The CNT facilitates a higher cooling rate at the surface, which traps more carbon in a harder bainitic structure. Meanwhile, at the range depth surface diffusion 30 µm till 60 µm, the specimen maintains a higher hardness consistent with surface diffusion depth (x = 34 µm) before converging toward the core hardness of 161 HV ± 15.1 at 100 µm. This convergence is critical, as it proves that the enhancement provided by the CNT nanofluid concentrated in the diffusion-affected zone near the surface, rather than altering the entire bulk of the steel.

sections.heading: Crack Growth Behavior
paragraphs: Figure  10  illustrates the crack length versus number of cycles (a-N) curves, comparing the crack propagation behavior for each untreated and quenching condition. The curves show an initially slow crack growth rate that gradually accelerates with increasing crack length and loading cycles, with each curve ending at the point of final fracture during crack growth test. The conventional oil and oil-based CNT nanofluid quenching media with different cooling rate showed similar crack growth trends in low-carbon steel. However, both performance significantly enhanced the fatigue life when compared to the untreated. Mechanistically, this improvement is governed by two main mechanisms. First, crack initiation is delayed by strengthened surface diffusion-affected layer formed during quenching especially in CNT nanofluid condition where increased carbon enrichment and higher near-surface hardness reduce local plastic strain accumulation and suppress microcrack nucleation. Second, once a crack forms, early-stage propagation is impeded by quench-induced the formation of a bainite phase and an increase in grain boundary dislocations, which increases grain boundary density and crack-path tortuosity, thereby enhancing resistance to crack advance. Fig. 10 Trend number of life cycles of untreated and treated specimens based on crack length increment observations

Crack growth typically progresses in three stages. Stage I corresponds to near-threshold crack growth and crack initiation behavior, where microstructure features and surface diffusion-hardened layer characteristics influence slow crack propagation. Meanwhile, Stage II is referred to as Paris regime, represents stable crack growth characterized by power-law relationship (C and m), between the crack growth rate (da/dN) and the stress intensity factor range (ΔK). Last, Stage III involves rapid and unstable crack propagation leading to final fracture. Therefore, this study specifically focused on transition from slow to stable crack propagation, comparing the threshold (ΔK th ) value, crack growth rate, and overall fatigue performance among untreated, conventional oil-quenched, and oil-based CNT nanofluid-quenched specimens.

The fracture surfaces of untreated and treated specimens of low-carbon steel are presented in Fig.  11 , highlighting a sharp notch, pre-crack, direction of crack growth, and fracture region. It is apparent from figure that the specimen quenched in oil-based CNT nanofluid is exhibiting the highest fatigue life reaching 34,464 cycles, more than double that of the untreated specimen (16,670 cycles) and slightly higher than the conventional oil-quenched specimen (28,800 cycles). These specimen trends align with the observed fracture surfaces, where the stable crack growth region reaches approximately 12 mm in the CNT nanofluid-quenched specimen, slightly longer than 11 mm for the conventional oil-quenched specimen and exceeding 10 mm in the untreated specimen. This suggests that a longer stable crack growth region in Stage II indicates an enhanced crack resistance, which directly contributes to the improved fatigue life. Fig. 11 Fracture surface for specimen ( a ) untreated, ( b ) oil quenching, and ( c ) oil-based CNT nanofluid quenching

The crack growth rate data at stable crack growth region obtained from untreated, conventional oil-quenched, and oil-based CNT nanofluid-quenched specimens were evaluated using the Paris model of Eq ( 1 ) and plotted along with the experimental results, as shown in Fig.  12 . The predictions made by the Paris model and the experimental trends showed strong similarities across all specimens, indicating that the Paris relationship effectively characterizes the crack propagation behavior in the Paris regime. The crack growth rate of the untreated specimen was larger than the conventional oil and oil-based CNT nanofluid-quenched specimens under the same ∆K which is primarily due to the presence of hard bainite phase transformations, a more homogeneous refined grain structure, and the formation of a surface diffusion-hardened layer. Moreover, the synergistic interaction of bainite–ferrite with residual ductility contributes to a toughness improvement and reduced brittleness, enabling the CNT nanofluid treated specimens to resist crack propagation more effectively. As shown in Fig.  12 c, the oil-based CNT nanofluid-quenched specimen exhibits markedly reduced scatter in crack growth data compared with the untreated and conventional oil-quenched conditions. This narrower scatter suggests that CNT-assisted quenching promotes more uniform cooling across the steel surface. In conventional oil quenching, the formation of a vapor blanket around the hot surface can generate local variations in heat extraction rate, producing microstructural heterogeneity. Incorporating CNT into the base oil can enhance heat transfer and destabilize the vapor film, enabling more efficient and more spatially uniform heat removal. As a result, cooling and transformation kinetics become more consistent, supporting the formation of a more stable near-surface hardened layer accompanied by measurable carbon enrichment. This improved microstructural uniformity yields a more homogeneous distribution of grain boundaries, hardened regions that act as consistent barriers to crack propagation, thereby reducing scatter in the da/dN–ΔK response [ 37 ,  38 ]. In turn, variability in local crack deflection and crack-tip plastic zone development is reduced, leading to a more repeatable crack growth behavior. Fig. 12 Crack growth rate described by the Paris model for ( a ) untreated, ( b ) oil quenching, and ( c ) oil-based CNT nanofluid quenching

The Paris model curve represents the relationship between the crack growth rate, da/dN, and the stress intensity factor range, ∆K. For the untreated low-carbon steel specimen, the crack growth rate in stable crack growth, Stage II ranged from 2.37 × 10 −8  to 8.06 × 10 −7  m/cycle, with the corresponding ΔK values varying between 34.4 and 51.8 MPa√m. In contrast, the specimens quenched in conventional oil and oil-based CNT nanofluid exhibited different behaviors. For the conventional oil-quenched specimen, crack growth rates ranged from 7.82 × 10 −8  to 6.49 × 10 −6  m/cycle, with ΔK ranging from 35.7 to 58.1 MPa√m. Meanwhile, the crack growth rate for the oil-based CNT nanofluid-quenched specimen ranged from 5.72 × 10 −8  to 5.17 × 10 −6  m/cycle, corresponding to a ΔK range of 35.1 to 59.5 MPa√m. These results proved that the crack growth behavior was significantly influenced by microstructural phase transformations, grain size refinement, and layer depth of carbon diffusion induced by different quenching media.

Table  5  presents the calculated Paris model parameters (C and m) and the threshold value (∆K th ) for the untreated, conventional oil, and oil-based CNT nanofluid-quenched specimens. According to [ 39 ], the reported ∆K th  values for untreated low-carbon steels typically range from 5 to 15 MPa√m which aligns well with the 14.1 MPa√m obtained in this study for the untreated specimen, showing a deviation of less than 10%. The results of the threshold value showed that the oil-based CNT nanofluid-quenched specimen exhibited the highest ΔK th , followed by conventional oil-quenched specimen and untreated specimen. The slope and exponent of the crack growth rate curve gained from the Paris model for oil-based CNT nanofluid specimen showed a distinct trend, where C value decreases from 3.0 x 10 -18  for the untreated specimen to 2.0 x 10 -20 , while the exponent m increases from 6.499 to 7.867. The reduction of the Paris constant C indicates a lower intrinsic crack growth rate for a given stress intensity factor range (ΔK). This behavior can be attributed to the refined microstructure produced by CNT-assisted quenching, which promotes the formation of fine upper bainite together with significant grain refinement and the development of a carbon-enriched surface diffusion with a hardened layer. These microstructural features increase the density of grain boundaries and introduce additional barriers to crack propagation. At the same time, the higher  m  value indicates greater sensitivity of crack growth rate to increase in ΔK, once the local microstructural resistance is exceeded. In the CNT nanofluid condition, the finer bainitic/ferritic morphology promotes crack-path tortuosity and crack-tip shielding, suppressing crack growth at lower ΔK. However, once ΔK becomes sufficiently large to overcome these barriers, crack growth accelerates more rapidly, producing a steeper Paris slope. Conversely, the untreated ferrite–pearlite microstructure with larger grains provides fewer obstacles to crack advance, leading to higher crack growth rates and a larger C value. The conventional oil-quenched specimen exhibits intermediate behavior, consistent with its moderate grain refinement, bainitic transformation, and surface hardening. Overall, the variation in the Paris parameters demonstrates that the crack growth behavior is strongly influenced by microstructural phase composition, grain size refinement, and the presence of a hardened surface diffusion layer induced by different quenching media. sections.heading: Prediction of Crack Growth Rate
paragraphs: A prediction-experiment comparison was performed to evaluate how accurately the Paris model represents the crack growth behavior of the untreated, conventional oil, and oil-based CNT nanofluid-quenched specimens. The predicted crack growth rates were plotted against the experimental values using a conservative scatter band, as shown in Fig.  13 . A conservative scatter band bounded by 2:1 and 1:2 correlation lines was used to assess the reliability of the predictions. This accuracy margin represents a commonly accepted tolerance in fatigue crack growth studies, where predictions errors within factor of two considered acceptable for engineering applications [ 40 ]. Although some deviations from the ideal 1:1 line were observed, the overall scatter trend demonstrates that the model captures the Paris regime behavior appropriately for all conditions. Among the three specimens, the oil-based CNT nanofluid-quenched specimen exhibited the most consistent agreement, as illustrated in Fig.  12 c, with its data points aligning closely along the 1:1 correlation line and showing the narrowest scatter band. This superior conformity indicates that the refined bainite–ferrite microstructure and the deeper diffusion-hardened layer developed during CNT nanofluid quenching contribute to a more stable crack growth response, thus enhancing the predictive accuracy of the Paris model. The predictions were considered reliable, as all crack growth rate points for the three specimens remained within the defined safety-factor boundaries. Fig. 13 Comparing the predicted crack growth rate from the Paris model with experimental data using the conservative scatter band for ( a ) untreated, ( b ) oil-quenched, and ( c ) oil-based CNT nanofluid-quenched specimens

In addition to scatter band analysis, a correlation assessment was performed using the coefficient of determination, R 2 , to evaluate the strength of the relationship between the predicted and experimental crack growth rates. Several researchers, including [ 41 ] and [ 42 ], have highlighted that R 2  values above 0.9 are considered very good, values above 0.8 are regarded as good, and in certain engineering applications, values above 0.6 may still acceptable despite the presence of prediction errors. It also noted that R 2  can be highly sensitive to the number of data points and the magnitude of variation within the dataset. Figure  14  illustrates the results of the Paris model showed strong agreement with the experimental data, and the correlation coefficients of 0.9401, 0.9667, and 0.9928 for the untreated, conventional oil, and oil-based CNT nanofluid of low-carbon steel specimens, respectively. These results indicate a strong linear correlation for all conditions, with the CNT nanofluid-quenched steel exhibiting the highest predictive accuracy. The R 2  values, all exceeding 0.9, confirm that the Paris model provides an excellent representation of the crack growth behavior for the investigated specimens. Fig. 14 Correlative coefficient between predicted crack growth rate using Paris model and from experimental data; ( a ) untreated, ( b ) oil-quenched, and ( c ) oil-based CNT nanofluid quenched

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study investigates the effects of microstructure and surface diffusion on the crack resistance of low-carbon steel using oil-based CNT nanofluid quenching with untreated specimen as a benchmark and conventional oil quenching specimen as comparison. The specimen quenched with CNT showed a transformation from pearlite and ferrite to a finer upper bainite–ferrite structure, unlike the coarser formation in conventional oil quenching. The rapid cooling rate from CNT nanofluid refined the grain size from 21 ± 0.99 µm to 10 ± 0.27 µm and slightly refined grain size compared to 12 ± 0.42 µm in conventional oil quenching. Surface diffusion analysis confirmed the highest carbon content 2.5 wt.% and depth of diffusion layer about 34 µm in CNT quenched specimen followed with 1.9 wt.% and 20 µm in conventional oil-quenched specimen. These improvement analysis in microstructure and surface diffusion contributed to significantly enhanced crack resistant and fatigue life more than double compared to untreated specimen and slightly higher than conventional oil-quenched specimen. In future, the same procedure involved water-based CNT nanofluid as quenching media can be conducted to evaluate its martensite performance in enhancing steel properties under cyclic loading condition.
